desc:
Houses stand on a straight street; houses[i] is the position of house i (the positions are in no particular order and may repeat). You may place exactly k mailboxes at integer positions of your choice. Every house walks to the closest mailbox. Return the smallest possible sum of all these walking distances.

houses = [1,4,8,10,20], k = 3  -> 5   (mailboxes at 4, 9, 20: distances 3 + 1 + 1 + 0)
houses = [2,3,5,12,18], k = 2  -> 9   (mailboxes at 3 and 12: distances 1 + 0 + 2 + 0 + 6)
houses = [7,7,7],       k = 1  -> 0
hints: After sorting the houses, the houses served by one mailbox form a consecutive group. So you are cutting the sorted list into k consecutive groups.
For one group, the best mailbox position is the median house of the group. Precompute cost[i][j], the total distance when houses i..j share one mailbox, using prefix sums.
Let dp[g][i] be the best cost for the first i sorted houses using g mailboxes: dp[g][i] = min over t of dp[g-1][t] + cost[t][i-1].
editorial: Sort the houses. Whenever two mailboxes exist, each house prefers the nearer one, and that makes the houses of one mailbox a contiguous block of the sorted order. So the task is to cut the sorted list into k blocks and to pay, for each block, the cost of the best single mailbox.

For a block, the sum of absolute distances is minimized at the median house (any point between the two middle houses works for even sizes). With prefix sums P of the sorted positions and median index m = (i + j) / 2, the cost is a[m]*(m-i) - (P[m]-P[i]) + (P[j+1]-P[m+1]) - a[m]*(j-m), available in O(1) after O(n) preparation, giving the table cost[i][j] in O(n2). The DP dp[g][i] = min(dp[g-1][t] + cost[t][i-1]) then takes O(k · n2) time. For the answer, only integer positions are needed, and the median is always a house position, so integer placement loses nothing.
